sentences.text: The name Longipteryx translates to "one with long feathers," derived from Latin and Ancient Greek roots.
This creature possessed a long snout that was longer than the rest of its head, ending in a few hooked teeth.
Unlike most birds of its time, Longipteryx possessed uncinate processes that strengthened its ribcage.
The humerus of Longipteryx was 1.56 times the length of its femur.
In life, Longipteryx measured approximately 15 cm in length, excluding the tail.
The holotype preserves impressions of body feathers, wing coverts, and down, but lacks preserved flight feathers.
The absence of long tail display feathers in all known specimens suggests that Longipteryx did not possess them.
In 2026, researchers described two new specimens that provided the best-preserved plumage and the first evidence of wing shape for the species.
The genus Longipteryx was first described by Zhang and colleagues in 2001.
Longipteryx lived during the Early Cretaceous, specifically the Aptian stage, approximately 120.3 million years ago.
Fossils of Longipteryx were found in the Jiufotang Formation in Chaoyang, Liaoning Province, China.
Longipteryx was initially interpreted by researchers as a piscivore or insectivore before evidence for frugivory was found.
A distinct order, Longipterygiformes, and family, Longipterygidae, have been proposed for Longipteryx.
Longipteryx is sometimes included in the clade Enantiornithes, specifically within Euenantiornithes, while other analyses classify it as basal to Enantiornithes.
The discovery of Longirostravis, which is closely related to Longipteryx, led researchers to suggest they form a specialized group of Euenantiornithes.
